task_title: Compliance with Air Traffic Control Clearances
area: Area III. Air Traffic Control (ATC) Clearances and Procedures
objective: By the end of this lesson you can copy an IFR clearance in C-R-A-F-T order, read it back correctly, and fly it from clearance delivery through departure, en route and arrival, including void times, climb via and descend via, cruise clearances, nonradar reports and lost communications.
why: A clearance is your contract with ATC for separation in the clouds. One misheard altitude or a clearance meant for another airplane can put you into traffic or terrain, so you must copy, question and fly it exactly.

key_terms.def: ATC authorization to proceed under stated conditions in controlled airspace, to prevent collisions between known aircraft. Not permission to break a rule.
The fix, point or location you are cleared to. Usually the destination airport.
Clearance copying order: Clearance limit, Route, Altitude, Frequency (departure), Transponder code.
Abbreviated clearance for your filed route. It does not include your filed en route altitude.
Time you must be airborne before. If you miss it, you lose authority to depart IFR and must tell ATC.
You may not depart on the IFR clearance until ATC gives a release time or more instructions.
The earliest time ATC lets you depart.
Block of airspace from the minimum IFR altitude up to the stated altitude. Also approval to fly an approach at the destination.
Start the climb or descent when you want, at any rate, and level off as you like. Once you leave an altitude, you can't go back.
Abbreviated clearance to fly a SID or STAR's lateral path and meet its published altitude and speed restrictions.
The time you can expect a clearance beyond a clearance limit. Key for lost communications.
Repeating key parts of a clearance (altitudes, vectors, runways) with your call sign so the controller can catch errors.

chunks.title: What a clearance is, and is not

body.p: You may not fly IFR in controlled airspace until you have filed an IFR flight plan and received an appropriate ATC clearance [[60:471|14 CFR 91.173]].

A clearance lets you proceed under set conditions so ATC can keep you apart from other known aircraft. It is not permission to break a rule, go below a minimum altitude or fly unsafely [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.123: once you have a clearance, don't deviate from it unless you get an amended clearance, an emergency exists, or you are following a TCAS resolution advisory. If you are not sure what the clearance says, ask ATC right away [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]].

head: Who
Main job with a clearance
rows: Pilot
Acknowledge it, request clarification or an amendment if it is unclear or unsafe, and comply promptly [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]]
Controller
Issue proper clearances, assign altitudes at or above minimum IFR altitudes, and correct wrong readbacks [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]] [[34:3|AIM 5-5-2]]
Both
The duties overlap on purpose, so one can catch the other's mistake [[34:2|AIM 5-5-1]]

body.p: Comply on receipt. When ATC gives a heading or a turn, start it promptly, finish it and hold the new heading. “Immediately” means expedite now for safety [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]].

The last clearance wins. If ATC changes or restates your altitude and leaves out earlier altitude restrictions, those restrictions are canceled, including SID and STAR altitude restrictions [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]].

callout.text: In VMC you still must see and avoid. Clearances separate you only from other IFR flights; VFR traffic may be out there without ATC knowing [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]].

check.q: ATC clears you to an altitude that is below the MEA on your route. Does the clearance make it legal?
check.a: No. A clearance is not authorization to deviate from any rule or minimum altitude. Request an amended clearance [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]].

chunks.title: Getting your clearance: clearance delivery, ground and data link

body.p: When you file, your flight plan goes to the Center computer. It prints flight strips for the tower, the departure radar facility and the first Center sector, about 30 minutes before your proposed departure time [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].
Most centers delete a flight plan that is not activated at least 2 hours after the proposed departure time. If you will be 2 hours or more late, tell ATC your new time [[33:339|AIM 5-1-13]].

head: Where you are
How you get the clearance
rows: Towered airport with clearance delivery
Call clearance delivery. Its frequency is on the approach and departure charts and in the Chart Supplement [[29:59|IPH 1-43]]. No clearance delivery? Ground control does it [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]
Pre-taxi clearance airport
Call clearance delivery or ground no more than 10 minutes before taxi [[33:343|AIM 5-2-1]]
PDC or CPDLC-DCL (data link)
Only for subscribers. No readback for a PDC; CPDLC needs a crew response. Call clearance delivery with any question [[33:343|AIM 5-2-2]] [[33:344|AIM 5-2-2]]
Airport without a tower
Use the frequency or phone number in the Chart Supplement. Say you are IFR and give departure and destination airports [[33:344|AIM 5-2-3]]

body.p: This figure comes from an older handbook. Where it says “A/FD,” use today's Chart Supplement [[29:60|IPH 1-44]].

Initial call when nothing has changed: call sign, location, “IFR” and the airport you expect clearance to [[33:347|AIM 5-2-6]]. The IFH sample flight: “Clearance Delivery, Cessna 1230A IFR to Gulfport Biloxi with information Kilo, ready to copy” [[23:322|IFH 10-31]].

callout.text: Listen to clearance delivery before you call. Hearing what departure procedure other flights get lets you write most of your clearance in advance [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].

check.q: At an airport with a pre-taxi clearance program, how early may you call for your clearance?
check.a: No more than 10 minutes before your proposed taxi time [[33:343|AIM 5-2-1]].

body.p: Clearances follow a set format: clearance limit, route (including any departure procedure), initial altitude, departure frequency and transponder code. One technique is to write C-R-A-F-T down the side of your page [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].

head: Letter
Item
Notes
rows: C
Clearance limit
Usually the destination airport, said with the word “airport.” It can be a NAVAID or fix [[33:275|AIM 4-4-3]]
R
Route
DP, transition and route. Normally the route you filed, but ATC may change it [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]
A
Altitude
Usually “maintain” an altitude, often with when to expect higher [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]] [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]]
F
Frequency
Departure control. May be left out if printed on the assigned DP [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8]]
T
Transponder
Squawk code. Computer generated, so you seldom know it ahead [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]

body.p: Write your expected clearance before you call. As the controller reads, check it against your notes. Cross out anything that changed and write the new item [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. Always make a written record of an IFR clearance [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]].

callout.text: IFH shorthand example: “CAF RH RV V18 40 SQ 0700 DPC 120.4” = cleared as filed, runway heading, radar vector to Victor 18, climb to 4,000, squawk 0700, departure control 120.4 [[23:340|IFH A-1]].

bullets: CAF = cleared as filed. v< = clearance void if not off by. EFC = expect further clearance [[23:340|IFH A-1]].
RH = runway heading. RV = radar vector. SQ = squawk. RTF = remain this frequency [[23:341|IFH A-2]].
Any shorthand system is fine, in any language, as long as you comply accurately. None is required by regulation [[23:340|IFH A-1]].

body.p: Before you accept a clearance, know where the named facilities are, plus the route and times between them [[23:295|IFH 10-4]].

check.q: Which C-R-A-F-T item can you almost never write before you call?
check.a: The transponder code. It is generated by computer [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].

body.p: Read back the parts with altitude assignments, vectors and runway assignments. This double check of the numbers catches misheard or wrong numbers [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]]. The IFH recommends reading your IFR clearance back to clearance delivery [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].

bullets: Include your call sign in every readback and acknowledgment, especially when similar call signs share the frequency [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].
Read back altitudes, altitude restrictions and vectors in the same order ATC gave them [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].
Don't read back altitudes printed on a charted DP or approach unless the controller states them [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].
Initial readback of a taxi, departure or landing clearance includes the runway, with left, right or center [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].
Read back all hold short instructions [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]].

body.p: Acknowledge frequency changes. If you just switch, the controller can't tell if you got it or lost your radio. Switch as soon as possible unless told to change at a time, fix or altitude [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]]. Don't switch to departure control until told to [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8]].

callout.text: Never abbreviate your call sign on initial contact or when similar call signs are on frequency. If in doubt, say “VERIFY CLEARANCE FOR” and your complete call sign [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].
Unless ATC authorizes it, you may not fly a clearance or instruction issued to another aircraft for radar control purposes [[60:451|14 CFR 91.123(e)]].

body.p: It is your job to accept or refuse a clearance [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]. A readback is not a substitute for understanding it.

check.q: ATC says “Cessna 5432K, turn left heading 240, descend and maintain 4,000.” What do you read back?
check.a: “Left heading 240, descend and maintain 4,000, Cessna 5432K.” Heading and altitude, in the order given, with your call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

chunks.title: Cleared as filed, departure procedures and climb via

body.p: If your filed route can be approved with little or no change, ATC issues an abbreviated clearance: “cleared to (destination) airport as filed” [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]]. If you or your company changed the flight plan, say so on initial call-up and request a full route clearance [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]] [[33:347|AIM 5-2-6]].

callout.text: “As filed” does NOT include your filed en route altitude. ATC states an altitude or tells you when to expect your filed altitude, verbally or in the DP [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]].

body.p: If a DP is to be flown, the controller names the DP, its number and the transition before “then as filed” [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]]. To use a DP you must have at least its textual description. If you can't or won't use one, file “NO DP” in remarks or tell ATC. Once you accept a DP, you must fly it [[23:296|IFH 10-5]].

The Birmingham Three is a radar vector SID: fly runway heading for vectors, maintain 5,000 or an assigned lower altitude, and expect your filed altitude ten minutes after departure. Its clearance delivery, ground and departure frequencies are printed on the chart [[23:297|IFH 10-6]].

head: SID clearance wording
What you do
rows: “Maintain (altitude)”
Used for a SID with no published crossing restrictions or a radar vector SID [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9]]
“Climb via SID”
Fly the lateral path and meet all published altitude and speed restrictions up to the top altitude [[33:355|AIM 5-2-9]] [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9]]
“Climb via SID except maintain (altitude)”
Same, but stop the climb at that altitude until cleared higher [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9]]
New altitude issued (“climb and maintain...”)
All earlier ATC altitude restrictions, including the SID's, are canceled. Speed and lateral path still apply [[33:357|AIM 5-2-9]]

body.p: On a climb via SID, tell departure on first contact your altitude leaving and any restriction not on the chart, for example “leaving two thousand, climbing via the Laura Two departure” [[33:357|AIM 5-2-9]].

callout.text: A radar departure does not relieve you of PIC duties. Have your receivers checked and tuned for the clearance before takeoff, stay oriented to the cleared route and log times over checkpoints [[23:297|IFH 10-6]].

check.q: You get “cleared to Albany airport as filed.” You filed 8,000 ft. May you climb to 8,000 after takeoff?
check.a: No. “As filed” does not include the filed altitude. Fly the altitude ATC or the DP gives you [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]].

chunks.title: Uncontrolled airports: void times, hold for release and release times

body.p: Departures from an airport without an operating control tower must get either a departure release (with a release and/or void time if needed) or a hold for release [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]]. If you can reach ATC, get the clearance before you are airborne [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]].

head: Restriction
What it means
Your action
rows: Clearance void if not off by (time)
You must be airborne before that time [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]]. Airborne exactly at the void time means the clearance is void [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]
Not off? Tell ATC your intentions as soon as possible, within the time ATC gives you, never more than 30 minutes after the void time [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]]
Hold for release
You may not depart on that IFR clearance until ATC gives a release time or more instructions [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]
You may still go VFR: cancel IFR first and use a VFR code. An IFR clearance may not be available later [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]
Released for departure at (time)
The earliest time you may depart [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]
Don't take off before it [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]
EDCT
Runway release time in a traffic management program [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]
Depart no earlier than 5 minutes before and no later than 5 minutes after it [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]

callout.text: No call within 30 minutes after the void time and you are considered overdue: search and rescue starts. Other IFR traffic at that airport is held until you call or 30 minutes pass [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]].

body.p: An expired void time does not cancel your flight plan. It takes away your authority to depart IFR until ATC issues a new release [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]]. Depart at or after the void time and you have no IFR separation and may violate 91.173. Departing VFR instead? Don't use the old IFR squawk [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]].

Help the controller by saying how soon you will be airborne [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. Other ways to get a clearance: FSS by phone or radio, a remote communications outlet, a UNICOM operator who relays it, or a ground communication outlet (GCO) [[29:59|IPH 1-43]] [[29:60|IPH 1-44]].

callout.text: Departing VFR to pick up your clearance in the air? You must stay VFR until cleared. If you accept a clearance below the minimum IFR altitude, terrain and obstacle clearance are yours until you reach it [[29:60|IPH 1-44]] [[33:280|AIM 4-4-9]].

check.q: Your void time passes while you are still doing the run-up. Is your IFR flight plan canceled?
check.a: No. You just lost authority to depart IFR. Call ATC within the allowed time (30 minutes at most) for a new release [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]].

chunks.title: En route: altitudes, cruise, pilot's discretion and speeds

body.p: “Maintain” means stay at that altitude. Ask for altitude changes before you need them [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]].

head: Clearance
How you fly it
rows: “Climb (descend) and maintain 6,000”
Start promptly. Optimum rate until 1,000 ft from the altitude, then 500 to 1,500 fpm. Can't do at least 500 fpm? Tell ATC [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]
“...at pilot's discretion”
Start when you like, any rate, level off as you like. Once you leave an altitude, you can't return to it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]
“Cross (fix) at or above (altitude)...”
Descent to the fix is at pilot's discretion, but you must meet the crossing restriction [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]] [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]]
“Cruise 5,000”

Any altitude from the minimum IFR altitude up to 5,000. Once you report leaving an altitude, you can't return without a clearance [[23:295|IFH 10-4]]. It also approves an approach at the destination [[34:332|P/CG C-11]]
“Expedite”
About your best rate. Canceled if the altitude is restated without “expedite” [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10]]

body.p: Need to level off early in a climb or descent? Tell ATC [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]].

**Speeds.** ATC assigns speeds in indicated airspeed, in 5 or 10 knot steps. Hold the assigned speed within plus or minus 10 knots [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12]]. If you can't accept a speed, tell ATC [[23:296|IFH 10-5]]. Tell ATC when your cruise TAS changes by 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater, from your flight plan [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]].

callout.text: “VERIFY ASSIGNED ALTITUDE AS 6,000” is a question, not a clearance. Confirm or tell the controller the altitude you are maintaining. Don't change altitude unless the controller authorizes it [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1]].

body.p: **VFR-on-top** is normally given only when you ask for it. You then fly VFR cruising altitudes and VFR cloud clearances, but still follow IFR rules such as minimum IFR altitudes, position reports and your clearance [[33:279|AIM 4-4-8]]. ATC does not separate you from other IFR traffic while VFR-on-top (outside Class B or a TRSA) [[33:282|AIM 4-4-11]].

check.q: You are cleared to “cruise 7,000.” You descend from 7,000, report leaving 6,000, and decide you'd like 6,000 after all. May you climb back?
check.a: No. After you report leaving an altitude in the block, you need a new clearance to return to it [[23:295|IFH 10-4]] [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]].

chunks.title: Arrival: STARs, descend via, holding and clearance limits

body.p: If your route includes a STAR, keep the last assigned altitude until ATC lets you descend to meet the published restrictions. That authorization may be “descend via” [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]]. To use a STAR you must have at least the approved chart; to refuse one, put “No STAR” in your remarks [[29:128|IPH 3-16]].

head: STAR clearance
What it allows
rows: “Cleared Tyler One arrival”
Lateral path and published speeds only. No descent [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1]]
“Cleared ... arrival, descend and maintain (altitude)”
Descend to that altitude, then hold it until cleared further [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1]]
“Descend via the Eagul Five arrival”
Descend at pilot's discretion while meeting all published altitude and speed restrictions [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1]]
Vectored off the STAR
STAR and its restrictions are canceled. Expect an altitude and maybe a speed [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]]

body.p: “Expect” altitudes and speeds on a STAR are for planning only. They are not restrictions unless ATC says them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]].

On a transition route, keep the last assigned altitude until you hear “cleared for the approach” [[23:299|IFH 10-8]]. If you can't fly the expected approach or want another, tell ATC right away [[23:299|IFH 10-8]].

**Clearance limits short of the airport.** When delay is expected, ATC gives holding instructions (unless charted), an EFC time and a delay estimate. No instructions before the fix? Hold in a standard pattern on the inbound course and ask [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]. Within 3 minutes of the limit with no further clearance, slow down to cross at or below holding speed [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]. Report time and altitude reaching the limit and when you leave it [[33:277|AIM 4-4-3]].

check.q: You are told “cleared Tyler One arrival.” The STAR shows crossing altitudes below you. May you start down?
check.a: No. That clearance is lateral only. You need a “descend via” or an assigned altitude [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1]].

chunks.title: Outside radar: position and other reports

body.p: Under IFR in controlled airspace you must keep a continuous listening watch. Report reporting points as required, unforecast weather and anything else that affects safety [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183]].

bullets: Report over each compulsory reporting point (solid triangle). Open triangles only on request [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2]].
On a direct route, report over each point that defines your route [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2]].
Stop routine reports when ATC says “radar contact.” Start again at “radar contact lost” or “radar service terminated” [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2]].
Passing a VOR, use the time of the first complete reversal of the TO/FROM flag [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2]].

callout.text: Position report items (AIM): identification, position, time, altitude, type of flight plan (not needed to Center or approach), ETA and name of the next point, name of the point after that, remarks [[33:376|AIM 5-3-2]] [[33:377|AIM 5-3-2]].

Outdated line in this figure: “Revised ETA of more than three minutes” is the old rule, also printed in IFH 10-8 [[29:105|IPH 2-45]] [[23:299|IFH 10-8]]. The current AIM says to report a corrected estimate when it is off by more than 2 minutes [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

body.p: Without a request, always report: leaving an assigned altitude, a VFR-on-top altitude change, unable 500 fpm, a missed approach, a TAS change of 5 percent or 10 knots, reaching and leaving a holding fix or clearance limit, lost nav or comm capability, and safety information [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].
When not in radar contact, also report leaving the FAF or outer marker inbound, and a corrected estimate any time your estimate is off by more than 2 minutes [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

callout.text: Malfunction report (91.187): aircraft identification, equipment affected, how much your IFR capability is impaired, and what help you want from ATC [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]].

check.q: Not in radar contact, you estimated KNOBS at 1532. You now expect 1535. Do you report it?
check.a: Yes. The error is 3 minutes, more than the 2 minutes the current AIM allows [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

body.p: Plan every IFR flight as if the radio could fail. At any point you must know what route to fly, what altitude, and when to leave the clearance limit [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

If the failure happens in VFR conditions, or you find VFR conditions later, stay VFR and land as soon as practicable [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(b)]]. That does not mean as soon as possible; you need not land at an unsuitable airport or just short of your destination [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]].

head: In IFR conditions
Rule
rows: Route (in this order)

Assigned in the last clearance; if vectored, direct from the failure point to the fix, route or airway in the vector clearance; the route ATC said to expect; the filed route [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)]]
Altitude
The HIGHEST of: last assigned, the minimum IFR altitude, or the altitude ATC said to expect, for the segment you are flying [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]
Clearance limit is an approach fix
Start descent and approach as close as possible to the EFC time, or if none, to your ETA from the filed or amended ETE [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)]]
Clearance limit is not an approach fix
Leave it at the EFC time, or if none, when you get there. Go to an approach fix and start the approach as close as possible to your ETA [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)]]

callout.text: Route: A-V-E-F (Assigned, Vectored, Expected, Filed), in that order [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)]]. Altitude: M-E-A (Minimum, Expected, Assigned), fly the highest for the segment you are on [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]].

body.p: An “expect” altitude counts only from the time or fix ATC gave. Hold the higher of your assigned and minimum altitudes until then, then climb [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1]]. AIM example: assigned 6,000, told to expect 8,000 at fix b, MEA 11,000 from c to d and 7,000 from d to e. Fly 6,000 to b, then climb to 8,000. Climb to 11,000 at c (earlier if an MCA requires it). At d, descend to 8,000, not 7,000, because 8,000 is the highest that applies [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1]].

bullets: Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]]. You may be outside radar coverage [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].
Try the last frequency, an FSS, New York Radio or San Francisco Radio, and 121.5. If you can, try all at once [[34:54|AIM 6-4-3]] [[34:55|AIM 6-4-3]].
Listen on NAVAID voice and try other aircraft [[23:334|IFH 11-9]].
Center frequency quiet? Wait at least 1 minute before deciding it has failed; backup transmitters usually switch within 60 seconds [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1]].

callout.text: STAR “expect” altitudes and speeds are not used for lost communications unless ATC told you to expect them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]].

check.q: In IMC, assigned 4,000, MEA 3,000, told “expect 6,000 ten minutes after departure.” Radio fails 3 minutes after takeoff. What altitude do you fly?
check.a: 4,000 until 10 minutes after departure, then climb to 6,000, the highest applicable altitude [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]] [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1]].

body.p: The PIC is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft. In an in-flight emergency that needs immediate action, you may deviate from any rule of Part 91 to the extent needed to meet it [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

head: After you...
You must...
rows: Deviate from a rule under 91.3(b)
Send a written report if the Administrator asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]
Deviate from a clearance in an emergency or for a TCAS RA
Notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]] and get an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]]
Get ATC priority without breaking a rule
Send a detailed report within 48 hours to the facility manager, if ATC asks [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]]

body.p: Whether a radio failure is an emergency is your call. Don't hesitate to use 91.3(b) if the situation calls for it [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]].

callout.text: You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you are doubtful about position, fuel, weather or anything else that could affect safety. Ask for help then, not later [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

check.q: You leave your assigned altitude in an emergency. What does 91.123 require next?
check.a: Notify ATC of the deviation as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]], then get an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: from “ready to copy” to on course

body.p: Based on the IFH sample flight [[23:322|IFH 10-31]] [[23:323|IFH 10-32]]:

bullets: 1. Before you call, check that your charts, DPs and GPS database are current. Use current editions and discard obsolete charts [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]]. The navigation database should be current for the whole flight [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]].
2. Copy ATIS. Write C-R-A-F-T with your expected items, then call clearance delivery “ready to copy” [[23:322|IFH 10-31]] [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].
3. Copy and read back. Review the DP and find any frequency or climb instruction on it, as the IFH pilot did (departure 123.8, climb to 2,100 before turning) [[23:322|IFH 10-31]].
4. Set it up: COM frequencies, NAV frequencies and course, GPS flight plan, and the squawk code. Identify each VOR by its Morse code or voice ID; that is the only positive way [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]].

5. Call ground (say you are IFR), taxi, and run the before-takeoff checklist [[23:322|IFH 10-31]]. On the runway: transponder to ALT, heading indicator agrees with compass, lights and pitot heat on [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].
6. When told, contact departure with your altitude so they can check your Mode C: “Birmingham Departure, Cessna 1230A, climbing through 2,700, heading 240” [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].

7. Join the cleared course: double the difference between the radial you are on and the one you want, for an intercept angle of 20° to 90°. Hold the intercept heading and lead the turn as the CDI centers [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
8. At each fix, note the time to track progress [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].

body.p: **SRM.** Single-pilot resource management means using every resource inside and outside the airplane, including ATC and automation [[30:56|RMH 8-3]]. Feeling rushed? Ask ATC for a delay or a vector to get time for checklists [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. A passenger can read a checklist or watch for something [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

callout.text: Checklists are a basic defense against errors [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Do the before-takeoff, climb, cruise and descent checklists at their phase of flight, not when you remember.

check.q: You are on the 160° radial and want to intercept the 205° radial. Using the IFH method, what is your intercept angle?
check.a: 90°. The difference is 45°, doubled is 90°, which is within the 20° to 90° limits [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

chunks.title: Risk: misheard, wrong, unflyable, or not for you

body.p: Unexpected clearances, controller errors, radio congestion and comm failure are common threats [[30:44|RMH 6-1]]. Your defenses are clear communication: agree on the plan, ask for clarification and question any inconsistency [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

head: Risk
What it looks like
What you do
rows: R1: Not fully understanding
Expectation bias: you hear the clearance you expected, not the one given [[30:45|RMH 6-2]] [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. “Reaching” and “leaving” sound alike [[29:109|IPH 2-49]]
Uncertain? Ask ATC immediately [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]]. Use plain English if needed [[23:55|IFH 2-4]]
R2: Wrong or unsafe clearance
A pilot read back 5,000 when cleared to 7,000. The controller didn't catch it, and the airplane nearly hit terrain [[29:121|IPH 3-9]]
Request an amended clearance if it would break a rule or put you in jeopardy [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]]. Question a heading or altitude you think is wrong [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]]
R3: Beyond your airplane or avionics
A speed, climb rate, climb gradient or RNAV procedure you can't fly

Say so: refuse excessive speeds [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]], report unable 500 fpm [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]], tell ATC if you can't make a DP's climb gradient [[29:59|IPH 1-43]], or “unable RNAV, request amended clearance” [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16]]
R4: Similar call signs
Another pilot takes your clearance (or you take theirs) using the last few digits [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]]
Use your full call sign, and say “VERIFY CLEARANCE FOR” your call sign if in doubt [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]]

body.p: You may ask for a different clearance if you have information that makes another action more practical, or if your equipment can't comply [[33:277|AIM 4-4-4]]. Tell ATC right away if your radios can't receive the signals needed for your clearance [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]].

callout.text: Off-airway direct clearances share terrain responsibility with you. Know the highest terrain and obstacles and where you are relative to them [[29:121|IPH 3-9]].
On a busy frequency, listen to the clearances given to other aircraft, especially ones with similar call signs, so you don't act on theirs [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5]].

check.q: ATC clears you to climb at a rate your heavily loaded airplane can't reach. What do you do?
check.a: Tell ATC you are unable at least 500 fpm, or request a different clearance because of equipment limits [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]] [[33:277|AIM 4-4-4]].

bullets: Reading back “line up and wait” correctly, then taking off without a takeoff clearance [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5]].
Mixing up “reaching” and “leaving” in a climb or turn clearance [[29:109|IPH 2-49]].
Abbreviating the call sign when similar call signs are on frequency [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].
Climbing to the filed altitude after a “cleared as filed” clearance [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]].
Lifting off exactly at the void time, or departing VFR on the old IFR squawk [[23:56|IFH 2-5]] [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]].
Changing altitude in response to “verify assigned altitude” [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1]].
Returning to an altitude already vacated under pilot's discretion or a cruise clearance [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]] [[23:295|IFH 10-4]].
Careless tuning and identification of a VOR [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].
Switching frequencies without acknowledging [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].
Keeping an old crossing restriction after an amended clearance left it out [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10]].

check.q: ATC says “line up and wait.” You read it back. May you start the takeoff roll?
check.a: No. Line up and wait is not a takeoff clearance. Wait for “cleared for takeoff” [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5]].

chunks.title: Reading the chart: a SID and a STAR behind the clearance

body.p: When ATC clears you to fly a SID, the chart holds the details. Read the route description box at the bottom first. On the LUFKIN SIX DEPARTURE it says to climb on the assigned heading for radar vectors to KYANN INT, maintain 5000, and expect the filed altitude 10 minutes after departure [[29:40|IPH Figure 1-22]].

Then check the notes and the take-off minimums box. This chart says radar is required. Runway 22 needs a standard minimum with a climb of 290 ft per NM to 1,500 ft, and Runway 17 is 300-1 [[29:40|IPH Figure 1-22]]. Make sure you can meet every note and minimum before you accept the SID.

A STAR works the same way. The title carries the name, here CHINS SEVEN ARRIVAL, and the STAR starts at CHINS intersection. Transitions bring you to CHINS from places such as Ephrata, Kimberly and Pendleton [[29:125|IPH Figure 3-11]]. The hold at RADDY helps controllers when weather causes delays. Radar vectors then lead to a north or south final approach course [[29:125|IPH Figure 3-11]].

Look for a lost communications line. On this chart it says to proceed direct to the SEA VORTAC after the AUBRN DME fix [[29:125|IPH Figure 3-11]]. A STAR clearance can be short, such as cleared as filed, then the arrival name and transition, maintain 10,000. The chart holds the rest [[29:127|IPH p 127]].

scenario.title: Void time, a look-alike call sign and a quiet radio
scenario.setup: You are in Cessna 5432K at a non-towered airport under a 900 ft overcast. You phone the clearance number from the Chart Supplement and copy: “Cessna 5432K cleared to Riverton airport via direct Eagle VOR, Victor 12, maintain 5,000, expect 7,000 ten minutes after departure. Departure 124.35, squawk 4521. Clearance void if not off by 1415. If not off by 1415, advise not later than 1430 of intentions.” It is 1407 and you still need to taxi and do a run-up. Later, on Center, a Cessna 3432K is on frequency, and you hear “Cessna 32K, descend and maintain 3,000.” The MEA on your airway is 4,000.

questions.q: You line up at exactly 1415. Can you go?
questions.a: No. You must be airborne before the void time; airborne exactly at the void time means the clearance is void [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. Tell ATC your intentions by 1430, as instructed. With no contact within 30 minutes after the void time, you are considered overdue and search and rescue starts [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]].

questions.q: The weather lifts to VFR and you decide to depart VFR after the void time. What about squawk 4521?
questions.a: Don't depart using the old IFR code [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]. The expired void time did not cancel your flight plan, so tell ATC your intentions [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]].

questions.q: On Center you hear “Cessna 32K, descend and maintain 3,000.” What is the risk and what do you do?
questions.a: It may be for Cessna 3432K. Similar call signs can make a pilot take another aircraft's clearance [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]], and you may not follow a clearance issued to another aircraft [[60:451|14 CFR 91.123(e)]]. Say “verify clearance for Cessna 5432K” [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].

questions.q: ATC confirms 3,000 is for you, but 3,000 is below the 4,000 MEA. Now what?
questions.a: A clearance never authorizes going below a minimum altitude. Question it and request an amended clearance [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]] [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]]. The controller should assign altitudes at or above minimum IFR altitudes [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]].

questions.q: Approach asks you to maintain 150 knots to the final approach fix. Your airplane can't safely do that. What do you say?
questions.a: Tell ATC you are unable. Refusing a speed adjustment your airplane can't safely fly is your responsibility and prerogative [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]] [[23:296|IFH 10-5]].

questions.q: Back to the departure: your radios fail in IMC 4 minutes after takeoff. What route, altitude and transponder code?
questions.a: Fly the assigned route: direct Eagle, Victor 12 [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)]]. Hold 5,000 (or the MEA if higher) until 10 minutes after departure, then climb to 7,000, the expected altitude [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]] [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1]]. Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].

skills.do: Copy, read back, interpret and comply with a simulated or actual clearance promptly, using AIM phraseology.
skills.practice: Pre-write C-R-A-F-T, copy practice clearances in shorthand, and read back altitudes, vectors and runways in the order given with your call sign [[23:56|IFH 2-5]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

skills.do: Set COM and NAV frequencies, identify NAVAIDs, and set the transponder code exactly as the clearance says.
skills.practice: After every readback, set and verify each radio and the squawk before taxi. Identify VORs by Morse code or voice ID [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]]. Acknowledge every frequency change [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].

skills.do: Use current paper or electronic charts, DPs, STARs and a current navigation database.
skills.practice: Check chart effective dates and the database cycle before each flight [[2:6|Chart Users' Guide p 6]] [[33:117|AIM 1-2-3]]. Have at least the text of any DP you accept [[23:296|IFH 10-5]].

skills.do: Intercept the courses, radials and bearings in the clearance in a timely manner.
skills.practice: Fly intercepts using the double-the-difference method (20° to 90°), leading the turn as the CDI centers [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

skills.do: Hold airspeed ±10 knots, heading ±10°, altitude ±100 ft, and track within ¾-scale CDI deflection (ACS IR.III.A.S5).
skills.practice: Trim before copying any amended clearance. Fly assigned speeds within ±10 knots [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12]].

skills.do: Use SRM: manage ATC, automation, passengers and time.
skills.practice: When rushed, ask ATC for a delay or vector, and use automation you understand to cut workload [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Give a passenger simple tasks like reading a checklist [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

skills.do: Do the right checklist items for each phase of flight.
skills.practice: Run the before-takeoff checklist holding short, then the lineup items: transponder ALT, heading indicator set, lights and pitot heat on [[23:322|IFH 10-31]] [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].

quiz.q: In the IFH technique C-R-A-F-T, what do the letters stand for?
options: Course, Route, Altimeter setting, Fuel, Time en route
Clearance limit, Route, Altitude, Frequency, Transponder
Clearance limit, Radar contact, Approach, Frequency, Taxi route
Clearance limit, Radial, Altitude restriction, Fix, Transponder code
quiz.why: The IFH format is clearance limit, route, initial altitude, departure frequency and transponder code [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].

quiz.q: Which parts of an airborne clearance does the AIM say you should read back?
options: Every word of the clearance, in full, including the frequency
Altitude assignments, vectors and runway assignments
Only the frequency and squawk code, since ATC checks the rest
Nothing, if you simply say “roger” and give your call sign
quiz.why: Read back altitudes, vectors and runway assignments as mutual verification [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]].

quiz.q: Your clearance says “void if not off by 1420.” Your wheels leave the runway at exactly 1420. Are you cleared?
options: No, it is void; you must be off before 1420
Yes, if you call departure right away after you are airborne
No, but you may continue if the weather is VFR once airborne
Yes, because 1420 is still within the time written in the clearance
quiz.why: If airborne exactly at the void time, the clearance is void. You must take off before it [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].

quiz.q: What does a “cleared to (destination) airport as filed” clearance NOT include?
options: Any departure procedure that ATC names in the clearance
The route of flight exactly as you filed it
Your destination airport as named in the clearance
Your filed en route altitude
quiz.why: “As filed” does not include the en route altitude in your flight plan. ATC states an altitude or when to expect one [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]].

quiz.q: ATC says “hold for release, expect 20 minutes departure delay.” What are your options?
options: Depart IFR as soon as you are ready if the weather is good enough
Depart IFR after waiting exactly 20 minutes from the controller's call
Wait for a release, or cancel IFR and depart VFR on a VFR code
Depart VFR on your IFR squawk code and pick up IFR clearance later
quiz.why: You may not depart on that IFR clearance until released. You may depart VFR after canceling IFR and using a VFR code [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]].

quiz.q: What does “descend via the Eagul Five arrival” authorize?
options: Immediate descent to the lowest altitude published on the STAR, then level off
Lateral navigation only; wait for ATC to give every descent altitude
Descent at pilot's discretion, meeting all published restrictions
A constant descent of 500 to 1,500 fpm down to the approach altitude
quiz.why: Descend via means descend at pilot's discretion and comply with all published altitude and speed restrictions [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]] [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1]].

quiz.q: Your radio fails in IMC while you are being vectored to join V12. Which route do you fly?
options: Keep flying the last assigned heading until you break out and see the ground
Direct from the point of failure to V12, the airway you were vectored to
The route you filed, joined from wherever you happen to be at the time
Direct to the destination airport, on the shortest line from your position
quiz.why: If being vectored, fly direct from the point of failure to the fix, route or airway in the vector clearance [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)]].

quiz.q: Not in radar contact, when must you give ATC a corrected estimate, by the current AIM?
options: Only when ATC asks
When the error is more than 5 minutes
When the error is more than 3 minutes
When the error is more than 2 minutes
quiz.why: The AIM requires a corrected estimate when it is off by more than 2 minutes (3 minutes in the North Atlantic) [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]]. The older IFH says 3 minutes [[23:299|IFH 10-8]].

quiz.q: In an emergency you deviate from your clearance. What must you do?
options: Notify ATC as soon as possible and get an amended clearance
Nothing, since emergencies need no notification or amended clearance
Send a written report to the FAA within 10 days of the deviation
Squawk 7600 and keep it until you land at your destination
quiz.why: Notify ATC of the deviation as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]] and obtain an amended clearance [[34:28|AIM 6-1-1]]. A written report under 91.3 is only on request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]].

quiz.q: Approach gives you “maintain 110 knots.” What speed range meets the AIM?
options: 105 to 115 knots
110 to 120 knots
90 to 130 knots
100 to 120 knots
quiz.why: Maintain assigned speeds within plus or minus 10 knots: 100 to 120 knots [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12]].

quiz.q: At which fix does the CHINS SEVEN ARRIVAL start?
options: RADDY
CHINS
AUBRN
HUMPP
quiz.why: The callout says the CHINS SEVEN ARRIVAL starts at CHINS intersection [[29:125|IPH Figure 3-11]].

quiz.q: Which fix is named as the common holding point on this STAR?
options: BRUKK
SUNED
AUBRN
RADDY
quiz.why: A callout says the hold at RADDY intersection often helps controllers manage traffic during weather delays [[29:125|IPH Figure 3-11]].

quiz.q: The lost communications line says that after the AUBRN DME fix you proceed:
options: Direct to the Yakima VOR
Direct to the SEA VORTAC
Direct to Boeing Field
Direct to the RADDY fix
quiz.why: The line reads After AUBRN DME FIX proceed direct SEA VORTAC [[29:125|IPH Figure 3-11]].

quiz.q: On the LUFKIN SIX chart, Runway 22 takeoff needs a climb of 290 ft per NM up to:
options: 300 ft
quiz.why: The take-off minimums box reads Rwy 22, standard with minimum climb of 290 ft per NM to 1500 [[29:40|IPH Figure 1-22]].

quiz.q: What does the note on the LUFKIN SIX chart say about radar?
options: Radar is not available
Radar is required
Radar is advised only
Radar contact ends at KYANN
quiz.why: The note reads RADAR Required [[29:40|IPH Figure 1-22]].

takeaways: A clearance separates you from known IFR traffic. It never authorizes breaking a rule or going below a minimum altitude.
Pre-write C-R-A-F-T, copy in shorthand, read back altitudes, vectors and runways with your full call sign.
“As filed” excludes your filed altitude. Climb via and descend via mean meet every published restriction.
Void time: be airborne before it. Missed it? Call ATC within 30 minutes. Hold for release: no IFR departure until released.
Lost comm in IMC: Assigned, Vectored, Expected, Filed for route; highest of Minimum, Expected, Assigned for altitude; squawk 7600.
Not sure, not safe, or not able? Ask ATC now, request an amended clearance, or say “unable.”
Hold ±100 ft, ±10°, ±10 knots and within ¾-scale CDI while complying.
cfi_notes: Outdated handbook line: IFH 10-8 and IPH Figure 2-68 (shown in chunk 9) say to report a revised ETA error of more than 3 minutes [[23:299|IFH 10-8]] [[29:105|IPH 2-45]]. The current AIM 5-3-3 (change of 1/22/26) says more than 2 minutes, with 3 minutes or more only in the North Atlantic. Teach 2 minutes [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

IFH Figure 2-16 still lists the Airport/Facility Directory (A/FD) and Flight Watch (EFAS, 122.0). The A/FD is now the Chart Supplement [[29:60|IPH 1-44]], and the current AIM no longer describes Flight Watch. Have students find clearance delivery, GCO and phone numbers in the current Chart Supplement, not the figure.

IFH 2-5 says items on a DP (altitude, departure frequency) are not included in the clearance. The AIM says the controller may omit the departure frequency if it is on the DP [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8]] and will state an altitude or when to expect one [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]]. Teach students to confirm the altitude every time.

Examiners commonly read a clearance with one change from what was filed and then ask the student to explain each item and its lost-comm meaning. Drill with real local clearances and BHM3-style “expect higher in 10 minutes” wording.

A common student error is reading back the whole clearance word for word but missing the altitude, or reading back charted DP altitudes. Coach the AIM list: altitudes, restrictions and vectors in order, plus runway, with call sign [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

Use the AIM 6-4-1 lost-comm examples on the whiteboard. Students often fly an “expect” altitude too early or use STAR expect altitudes, which don't apply unless ATC said to expect them [[33:393|AIM 5-4-1]].

Climb via and descend via are rarely issued to piston trainers, but they appear in clearances at busy airports and in knowledge questions. Have students say the required initial report on a climb via SID [[33:357|AIM 5-2-9]].
gaps: No FAA source has a common-errors list for complying with ATC clearances; the Common errors chunk is built from AIM, IPH and IFH cautions.
Setting a specific GPS, audio panel or transponder (S2) depends on the airplane's POH/AFM supplements, which are not in these sources.
Local clearance delivery phone numbers, GCO frequencies and airport-specific procedures come from the current Chart Supplement, which is not uploaded.

The IFH and IPH chart figures (2010 cycle) are for teaching only; current SIDs and STARs, including real climb via and descend via examples, must come from the current Terminal Procedures Publication.
PDC and CPDLC-DCL are described only for subscribing operators; there is no GA-specific data link guidance in these sources.

activities.intro: On a DP, each NAVAID box shows the frequency (FREQ), identifier, Morse Code and latitude, longitude. The chart's effective dates run up the side margins, and the departure airport is the circled runway symbol. Drag each name to its numbered pin.

activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

Missed it? Tell ATC within 30 minutes or search and rescue may start
After it expires, don't depart VFR on the IFR squawk

Comes with expected departure delay information
The earliest time you may take off

activities.title: From climb via to a crossing restriction
activities.intro: You are flying Cessna 5432K IFR from a towered airport. You filed 8,000 ft. Clearance delivery reads: “Cessna 5432K, cleared to Albany airport via the Hilltop Two departure, Eagle transition, then as filed. Climb via SID. Departure frequency 124.35, squawk 4521.” The Hilltop Two has a top altitude of 7,000 and a published restriction: cross RIVET at or below 3,000.

steps.s: Your tablet with the Hilltop Two just died, and you have no other copy of the chart or its text.
options: Tell ATC you can't accept the DP; request an amended clearance
Accept it and plan to ask departure for vectors after takeoff
Accept it and fly runway heading until you can see the chart again
Read it back and look up the route on another source after takeoff
steps.why: To use a DP you must have at least its textual description. If you can't use one, tell ATC, and once you accept a DP you must fly it [[23:296|IFH 10-5]].

steps.s: Your backup tablet works and you have the chart. What do you read back?
options: “Cleared to Albany airport via the Hilltop Two departure, Eagle transition, then as filed, climb via SID, departure 124.35, squawk 4521”
“Cleared to Albany airport, Hilltop Two, Eagle transition, then as filed, climb via SID, cross RIVET at or below 3,000, then 7,000, 124.35, squawk 4521, Cessna 5432K”
“Cleared to Albany airport, Hilltop Two, Eagle transition, then as filed, climb via SID, climb and maintain 8,000, 124.35, squawk 4521, Cessna 5432K”
“Cleared to Albany airport, Hilltop Two, Eagle transition, then as filed, climb via SID, 124.35, squawk 4521, Cessna 5432K”
steps.why: Don't read back altitudes printed on a charted DP unless the controller states them, and include your call sign [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]. “As filed” does not include your filed altitude [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]].

steps.s: After takeoff, tower tells you to contact departure. You are passing 1,800 ft. What is your first call?
options: “Departure, Cessna 5432K, with you, Hilltop Two departure, request a higher altitude when ready”
“Departure, Cessna 5432K, leaving one thousand eight hundred, climbing to eight thousand as filed”
“Departure, Cessna 5432K, leaving one thousand eight hundred, climbing via the Hilltop Two departure”
“Departure, Cessna 5432K, request higher altitude, climbing on the Hilltop Two departure”
steps.why: On a climb via clearance, tell ATC on first contact the altitude you are leaving and that you are climbing via the SID [[33:357|AIM 5-2-9]].

steps.s: At 2,600 ft, short of RIVET, departure says: “Cessna 5432K, climb and maintain 5,000.” What do you do?
options: Hold 3,000 until past RIVET, then climb to 5,000 as the SID requires
Climb to 5,000 now and turn direct to Eagle, leaving the SID's path
Climb to 5,000 now and keep flying the SID's lateral path
Ask ATC to repeat it and explain, because it conflicts with the SID restriction
steps.why: A new ATC altitude cancels earlier altitude restrictions, including those published on the SID. You still fly the SID's lateral path and speed restrictions [[33:357|AIM 5-2-9]].

steps.s: Later, level at 8,000 and 40 NM from KNOBS, you hear: “Cessna 5432K, cross KNOBS at or above 6,000, descend and maintain 4,000.” What is your plan?
options: Descend promptly to 4,000 now and cross KNOBS at 4,000, ahead of the restriction
Descend at your discretion, cross KNOBS at or above 6,000, then promptly to 4,000
Stay at 8,000 well past KNOBS, then descend to 4,000 whenever convenient
Descend to 6,000 now and wait there for another clearance before going lower
steps.why: With a crossing restriction, the descent to the fix is at pilot's discretion, but you must meet the crossing altitude, so you can't be below 6,000 at KNOBS. After the fix, descend at the suggested rates to the assigned altitude [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]] [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]].

activities.title: True or false: en route and arrival clearances
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Under “descend at pilot's discretion, maintain 6,000,” you may level off at 8,000 for a while.
cards.why: Yes. Pilot's discretion allows temporary level-offs, but once you leave an altitude you can't return to it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]].

cards.s: “Cleared Tyler One arrival” lets you descend to the STAR's published crossing altitudes.
cards.why: No. That is a lateral clearance only; no descent is authorized [[33:394|AIM 5-4-1]].

cards.s: A cruise clearance also approves an approach at the destination airport.
cards.why: Yes. It is approval to proceed to and make an approach at the destination [[34:332|P/CG C-11]].

cards.s: When ATC asks “verify assigned altitude as 7,000,” you should climb to 7,000.
cards.why: No. Confirm or correct the altitude. Don't change altitude unless the controller authorizes it [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1]].

cards.s: If an amended clearance restates your altitude and leaves out an earlier crossing restriction, that restriction no longer applies.
cards.why: Yes. Omitted altitude restrictions are canceled when the altitude to maintain is changed or restated [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]].

cards.s: Within 3 minutes of a clearance limit with no further clearance, you should start slowing to holding speed.
cards.why: Yes. Cross the fix initially at or below maximum holding airspeed [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]].

activities.title: Clearance numbers: crossings, rates and times
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You are at 9,000 ft, cleared “cross KNOBS at 5,000.” Groundspeed is 120 knots and you plan to descend at 500 fpm. At the latest, how many NM before KNOBS must you start down?
items.why: Altitude to lose: 9,000 - 5,000 = 4,000 ft. Time: 4,000 / 500 = 8 minutes. Distance: 120 knots is 2 NM per minute, so 8 x 2 = 16 NM. When to start is your choice, but you must make the crossing [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]] [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]].

items.q: You are at 8,000 ft and 12 NM from LAKEV, cleared to cross it at or below 5,000. Groundspeed is 150 knots. What is the minimum descent rate if you start now?
items.why: Altitude to lose: 3,000 ft. 150 knots is 2.5 NM per minute, so 12 / 2.5 = 4.8 minutes. 3,000 / 4.8 = 625 fpm. You must comply with the crossing altitude as part of the clearance [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]].

items.q: Heavy and hot, your airplane climbs 2,100 ft in 6 minutes. What is your climb rate? (If it is under 500 fpm, you must tell ATC.)
items.why: 2,100 / 6 = 350 fpm. That is less than 500 fpm, so advise ATC [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]] [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

items.q: Not in radar contact, you passed ACORN at 1410 and gave ATC a BIRCH estimate of 1425 (30 NM ahead at 120 knots). Your groundspeed is now 100 knots. What is your new BIRCH estimate (type it as hhmm)?
items.why: 30 NM at 100 knots = 0.3 hour = 18 minutes. 1410 + 18 = 1428. That is 3 minutes off, more than 2, so report the corrected estimate [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

items.q: Lost comm in IMC. Your clearance limit is the IAF and you got no EFC. You departed at 1312 with a filed ETE of 1 hour 25 minutes. When should you start the approach (hhmm)?
items.why: ETA = 1312 + 1:25 = 1437. With no EFC, start descent and approach as close as possible to the ETA calculated from the filed or amended ETE [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)(i)]].

activities.title: From clearance to departure
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Call clearance delivery “ready to copy” and copy the clearance
Read back the clearance and review the DP
Set up frequencies and navigation equipment for the departure
Call ground, noting that you are IFR, and taxi
Complete the before-takeoff checklist and run-up, then tell tower you're ready
After takeoff, contact departure when told, giving your altitude

activities.title: Read the SID chart
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.
activities.why: The title names the procedure. Frequencies are listed at the top left, the note says radar is required, take-off minimums sit under the sketch, and the route description is in the box at the bottom. The Little Rock transition ends at the LIT VORTAC [[29:40|IPH Figure 1-22]].

final_quiz.q: Your clearance reads “void if not off by 1530, if not off by 1530 advise not later than 1600 of intentions.” You can't depart. If you never call, when may search and rescue begin?
options: After 1600
After 1630
final_quiz.why: ATC's notification time can't exceed 30 minutes after the void time. No contact by then and you are considered overdue and SAR starts [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]].

final_quiz.q: You get an EDCT of 1442. What is the acceptable departure window?
options: Any time before 1442
final_quiz.why: Depart no earlier than 5 minutes before and no later than 5 minutes after the EDCT [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]].

final_quiz.q: You filed a cruise TAS of 150 knots. Which actual TAS change must you report to ATC without being asked?
options: A drop to 146 knots
A drop to 143 knots
A rise to 155 knots
A drop to 138 knots
final_quiz.why: Report changes of 5 percent or 10 knots, whichever is greater. 5% of 150 is 7.5 knots, so 10 knots applies; 138 is 12 knots slower [[33:377|AIM 5-3-3]].

final_quiz.q: ATC: “Descend and maintain 4,000.” You are at 9,000, with no pilot's discretion. How should you descend?
options: At any rate you like, starting whenever it is convenient for you
At exactly 500 fpm the whole way down, from the moment you are cleared
Promptly, at an optimum rate to 5,000, then 500 to 1,500 fpm to 4,000
Promptly, at 1,500 fpm or more all the way down to 4,000 without slowing
final_quiz.why: Start promptly, use an optimum rate to 1,000 ft above the assigned altitude, then 500 to 1,500 fpm [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]].

final_quiz.q: You were cleared “cross Delta VOR at 10,000, maintain 6,000.” Before Delta, ATC says “turn right heading 180, vector ILS runway 36, maintain 6,000.” What about the Delta crossing?
options: It is canceled, because the amended clearance omitted it
It applies only if you actually pass directly over Delta at some point
Ask ATC before descending below 10,000, since the restriction is unresolved
It still applies; you must cross Delta at 10,000 before descending further
final_quiz.why: When ATC restates the altitude and omits earlier restrictions, those restrictions are canceled [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]] [[33:282|AIM 4-4-10]].

final_quiz.q: Before takeoff you get “Climb via SID except maintain 9,000.” What do you do?
options: Fly the SID to its top altitude, then descend back down to 9,000
Climb directly to 9,000 and ignore the SID's lateral path and restrictions
Fly the SID path and its restrictions, stopping the climb at 9,000
Fly runway heading up to 9,000, then join the SID's lateral route
final_quiz.why: Comply with the SID lateral path and published speed and altitude restrictions while climbing to the stated altitude, then stop there [[33:356|AIM 5-2-9]].

final_quiz.q: In IMC, assigned 5,000, the MEA ahead rises to 7,000, and you were never told an expected altitude. Your radios fail. What altitude for the 7,000 MEA segment?
options: 5,000, the last altitude assigned in your clearance
Your filed altitude, because no expected altitude was given to you
6,000, halfway between your assigned altitude and the MEA ahead
7,000, the minimum IFR altitude for that segment
final_quiz.why: Fly the highest of the assigned, minimum IFR, or expected altitude for the segment being flown. Here the MEA is highest [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]] [[34:54|AIM 6-4-1]].

final_quiz.q: Lost comm, your clearance limit is the IAF for the approach. No EFC was given. Your ETA from the filed ETE is 1452, but you reach the IAF at 1440. When do you start the approach?
options: Right away at 1440
When you hear the ATIS
At 1500, 20 minutes after reaching the IAF
As close as possible to 1452
final_quiz.why: With the clearance limit at an approach fix and no EFC, start descent and approach as close as possible to the ETA from the filed or amended ETE [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: You depart VFR from a non-towered field and accept an IFR clearance while below the MIA. Who is responsible for terrain clearance until you reach it?
options: You, until you reach the minimum IFR altitude
Nobody, because you are on an IFR clearance and ATC is handling you
The departure controller only, from the moment you take off and call
ATC, once you are radar identified and the controller has you in contact
final_quiz.why: When you accept a clearance below the MEA/MIA/MVA/OROCA, terrain and obstruction clearance are your job until you reach it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your GPS fails just after ATC assigns an RNAV SID. What does the AIM say to do?
options: Fly the SID using your VOR receiver instead, without telling ATC
Tell ATC you are unable RNAV and request an amended clearance
Say nothing to ATC and just fly runway heading until the GPS recovers
Squawk 7700 and continue to fly the route you originally filed
final_quiz.why: If unable to meet RNAV procedure requirements, advise ATC as soon as possible, e.g. “unable RNAV, request amended clearance” [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16]].

final_quiz.q: Cessna 5432K hears “Cessna 32K, cleared ILS runway 9 approach” while a Cessna 3432K is also holding nearby. Best response?
options: Read it back with “32K” and start the approach
Stay silent; the other pilot will answer
“Verify clearance for Cessna 5432K”
Start the approach and report the procedure turn
final_quiz.why: When in doubt about identity, say “VERIFY CLEARANCE FOR” and your complete call sign [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]]. You may not fly another aircraft's clearance [[60:451|14 CFR 91.123(e)]].

final_quiz.q: You are on the 090° radial and want to intercept the 105° radial. With the IFH method, what intercept angle do you use?
final_quiz.why: Difference 15°, doubled is 30°, which is within the 20° to 90° limits [[23:257|IFH 9-14]].

final_quiz.q: You are in IMC on an IFR clearance and ATC hasn't spoken for a while. The frequency seems dead. What should you do first?
options: Squawk 7600 immediately, before trying any other frequency or radio
Climb to the highest MEA on the route and keep monitoring that frequency
Wait at least 1 minute, then try other frequencies or an FSS
Turn toward the nearest VFR airport and descend out of the clouds
final_quiz.why: Backup radios usually switch within 60 seconds, so wait at least 1 minute. Then try the last controller, another sector, or an FSS [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1]].

final_quiz.q: The LUFKIN SIX route description says to expect the filed altitude:
options: Upon reaching 1,500 ft
10 minutes after departure
After passing the LFK VORTAC
At the KYANN intersection
final_quiz.why: It reads Expect filed altitude 10 minutes after departure [[29:40|IPH Figure 1-22]].

final_quiz.q: The primary arrival airport for the CHINS SEVEN ARRIVAL is:
options: Boeing Field/King County
Yakima Air Terminal
Sea-Tac International
Ephrata Municipal
final_quiz.why: The callout names Seattle-Tacoma International as primary. Other airports, such as Boeing Field, may also be served [[29:125|IPH Figure 3-11]].

final_quiz.q: You are not sure you heard a clearance altitude correctly. What does 14 CFR 91.123 say to do?
options: Wait until ATC corrects you
Climb to the MEA and say nothing
Fly the altitude you believe you heard
Immediately ask ATC for clarification
final_quiz.why: When a pilot is uncertain of a clearance, that pilot shall immediately request clarification from ATC [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You deviate from a clearance because of a TCAS resolution advisory. What must you do under 14 CFR 91.123?
options: Notify ATC as soon as possible
Nothing, because ATC saw it on radar
Return to the old altitude without a call
File a written report within 10 days
final_quiz.why: A pilot who deviates because of an emergency or a TCAS RA must notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]].
